newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE - Pakistan's Imran scores with anti-corruption pledge.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pakistan's Imran scores with anti-corruption pledge.

text.p: Imran Khan, Pakistan's former cricket captain, cuts a dashing figure among the shabby villagers whose votes he is seeking in the February 3 election.
Wearing a dark blue half-coat over a khaki shalwar kameez (long shirt and baggy trousers), a smiling Imran gets his message across in simple language that his audience understands.

A political novice, Imran portrays himself as a new force that can clean up a system he says has been sullied by former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, President Farooq Leghari and Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari.

"Mian (Sharif), Bibi (Bhutto), Zardari and Leghari are all the same," he tells a few dozen youths at one village meeting near Islamabad. "They have robbed the country, they have robbed the people. Now let's put a stop to it."
Imran promises that he will topple a political system that he says robs the poor and enriches the wealthy.
This is a bold ambition in Pakistan, where Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) and Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) have dominated politics since military rule ended in 1988.

Despite popular perceptions that corruption flourished under both leaders, Bhutto and Sharif are still front-runners in the election called by Leghari after he sacked Bhutto's government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule.
Leghari pledged that an anti-corruption drive by the caretaker government he named to oversee the elections would clean up the system and bar tainted politicians from the polls.

Yet no important political figures, with the exception of Zardari, who ruled himself out from his jail cell, have been disqualified and the slow progress made by the Ehtesab (Accountability) Commission has disappointed many Pakistanis.
Imran has now seized on this perceived failure to demand that Leghari resign to ensure free and fair elections.

He alleges that the president has made a secret deal with Sharif, under which the PML leader will be allowed to form the next government on condition that he accepts the advice of a newly formed Council for Defence and National Security.
Sharif and Leghari, who is chairman of the civilian-military council, deny any such deal.
Imran, who formed his Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) only nine months ago, is a candidate in nine constituencies in his bid for a seat in the 217-member National Assembly.
Disenchantment with established politicians should help Imran, who built a cancer hospital in Lahore after ending his cricket career by leading Pakistan to a 1992 World Cup triumph.
Imran, still lean and athletic at 43, looks exhausted as he campaigns from village to village, but stays cheerful and speaks passionately of Pakistan's need for reform.
"I can topple these big names, but only with your support, just as I built the cancer hospital with your help," he says.
Imran's hospital fund-raising campaign, which took him to cities, towns and villages across Pakistan, elicited an enthusiastic response which helped propel him into politics.
Many ordinary people like him, but doubt he will have much electoral impact. "He has yet to prove his political worth," says a farmer at an Imran rally in Sihala, south of the capital.
"He is standing in Islamabad, but the real neck-and-neck contest (there) is between the PPP and the PML candidates," says the farmer. "He may get five percent of the votes."
Imran's fans realise his party's shortcomings in terms of funds, experienced activists and organisation. "It will come with time. We are doing the best we can," says one volunteer.
Imran, who abandoned his playboy past after rediscovering his Islamic roots, married Jemima Goldsmith, daughter of Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith in 1995.
The wealthy Jemima, a convert to Islam, has taken a modest part in her husband's election campaign, attending a few women's meetings that she addresses in hesitant Urdu.

Pakistan's most glamorous couple, who had a son last year, have had to cope with embarrassing allegations by one of Imran's ex-girlfriends, heiress Sita White, that he is the father of her four-year-old daughter Tyrian.
Imran has dismissed the allegations, saying they are part of a campaign by his political opponents to damage his reputation.
"Sita's accusations have definitely hurt Imran, especially with conservative women voters," says a rueful party worker.
